title: Payment System
summary: Move money through a provider you do not control, and be able to prove afterwards exactly what happened. The one design in this repository where eventual consistency is not a trade you may make about the outcome — only about when you find out.

versions.label: 500K payments/day
versions.trigger: Launch. The checkout request calls the provider, waits for an approval and writes "paid" on the order.
versions.note: Correct at this size, and it already contains the failure that shapes everything after it: the provider times out. You now do not know whether the card was charged. Not "it failed" — unknown. Every subsequent version exists to make that unknown recoverable.

versions.label: 1M/day · idempotency keys
versions.trigger: A customer's phone lost signal mid-checkout and the app retried. They were charged twice and the refund took nine days.
versions.note: Three details decide whether this works. The key is generated by the CLIENT before the first attempt and reused on every retry — a server-generated key is a new payment each time. The stored value is the RESPONSE, not a flag, so a retry can be answered without touching the provider. And the same key with a different body is rejected, not replayed, because that is a bug in the caller rather than a retry. Note the store is a cylinder: losing this costs money, so it is not a cache.

versions.label: 2M/day · the saga
versions.trigger: Authorise, capture and record are three steps across two systems and no transaction spans them. The checkout request was holding a socket open for all three.
versions.note: A saga has no rollback, only compensation: the compensating action for an authorisation is a void, and for a capture it is a refund — both are new operations against the provider, and both can themselves fail. That is why the API now returns 202 and "pending" rather than 200 and "paid". Returning a result you do not yet have is the most expensive lie this system can tell.

versions.label: 3M/day · double-entry ledger
versions.trigger: Finance asked what the outstanding balance was and three services gave three different answers. A boolean paid column on an order is not an accounting record.
versions.note: Every movement is at least two entries that sum to zero, and nothing is ever updated — a mistake is corrected by a reversing entry, so the error and its correction are both visible forever. The ledger becomes the source of truth and the payment record becomes a projection of it. When those two disagree, the ledger is right by definition, and that rule is what makes the disagreement resolvable instead of a debate.

versions.label: 5M/day · reconciliation
versions.trigger: The provider's monthly statement was GBP 4,000 away from the ledger. Neither side was wrong: 61 payments had succeeded at the provider and had never been recorded here.
versions.note: The key insight of the whole design. You cannot make the external provider transactional, so the ledger cannot be correct by construction — it has to be RECONCILABLE. Three outcomes: in ours and not theirs, in theirs and not ours, in both with different amounts. Each has a defined resolution, and the ones that do not resolve automatically go to a human. Reconciliation is not a cleanup job bolted on afterwards; it is the correctness mechanism.

versions.label: 5M/day · webhooks
versions.trigger: The provider's captured event arrived before its authorised event, and a retried webhook applied the same capture twice.
versions.note: Four rules, all mandatory. Verify the signature before parsing anything, because this endpoint is public. Dedupe on the provider's event id, because delivery is at-least-once. Compare against the state machine and ignore any transition already passed, because delivery is unordered. And treat the body as a HINT rather than as truth — the safe handler fetches the payment from the provider by id and acts on that.

versions.label: 5M/day · refunds and partial captures
versions.trigger: A customer returned one item from a three-item order. The system could refund all of it or none of it, because it had recorded one amount and one state.
versions.note: A payment stops being a state and becomes a set of movements: authorised 49.99, captured 29.99, refunded 9.99, and the remaining 20.00 of the authorisation expires unclaimed. Only the ledger can express that. Summing an append-only ledger on every page load is expensive, so the balance is materialised — and because it can be rebuilt by replaying the ledger, it is drawn dashed. That is the difference between a cache and a store, on the page where it matters most.

versions.label: Provider degraded · unknown outcomes
versions.trigger: Design review: the provider times out on 8% of captures, and most of those captures actually succeeded.
versions.note: A timeout is not a failure, it is an absence of information, and the two must never be conflated. Never retry a capture blindly; re-query the provider by idempotency key and act on the answer. Never mark the payment failed, because roughly 90% of these succeeded. The ledger needs an account that means UNKNOWN — a suspense account — so the books still balance while you find out. Webhooks close most of them within minutes, reconciliation closes almost all of the rest, and a handful reach a human. That last handful is not a defect in the design; it is the design admitting what it cannot know.

flows.label: Charge inline
flows.outcome: Nine hundred milliseconds of somebody else's system on the critical path, and no answer at all when it times out.

flows.label: A retried request
flows.outcome: The key has been seen, so the stored response is replayed and the provider is never called. One charge, however many times the client asks.

flows.label: Run the saga
flows.outcome: The customer is answered in 35 ms with pending. Authorise and capture happen behind the queue, each step idempotent and each retryable on its own.

flows.label: Post to the ledger
flows.outcome: Debit one account, credit another, sum to zero, append only. The payment record is updated afterwards and is only a convenience.

flows.label: Reconcile against settlement
flows.outcome: Match every line. In ours and not theirs, in theirs and not ours, or in both with different amounts — the third is the one that costs an afternoon.

flows.label: Handle a provider webhook
flows.outcome: Verify, dedupe on the event id, ignore anything the state machine has already passed, then post. An unguarded handler applies the same capture twice.

flows.label: Refund part of a payment
flows.outcome: A reversing entry, not an edit. The original capture stays in the ledger forever and the refund sits beside it.

flows.label: Capture times out
flows.outcome: Post to suspense, re-query by idempotency key, wait for the webhook, then for reconciliation, then hand it to a human. Four chances to learn the truth, in increasing order of cost.

failures.effect: No money moves. From V3 the saga holds intents and retries when the provider returns, so the customer sees pending rather than declined — the difference between a delayed sale and a lost one. But nothing can be completed, and a second provider is the only real answer.

Retries stop being recognised and every one becomes a fresh charge. This must fail CLOSED: refuse the payment rather than risk charging twice. It is the one component here that looks like a cache and is drawn as a store, because losing it costs money rather than latency.

Intents are accepted by the API and never executed, so customers sit at pending indefinitely. Survivable only if the API refuses to acknowledge an intent it could not enqueue — otherwise you have promised to take money you have no record of needing to take.

Sagas stop mid-flight: some authorised and not captured, some captured and not recorded. Nothing is lost because the queue holds the work, but every step of the recovery must be idempotent, and this is the outage that proves whether it actually is.

No movement can be recorded, so no payment may proceed. A charge you cannot record is a charge you cannot reconcile, refund or account for, and taking it anyway converts a technical outage into an accounting one.

Nothing breaks today. Divergence accumulates silently and you discover it at month end, which is precisely the failure this component exists to prevent — the most dangerous kind, because the dashboard stays green.

Provider events are missed and payments linger in pending. Most providers retry for hours and reconciliation catches whatever they do not, which is the second reason reconciliation is load-bearing rather than hygiene.
Customers cannot see a balance. No money is affected and the projection is rebuilt by replaying the ledger. This is what safe to lose actually means, and it is why this node alone is dashed.

The state machine is unreadable, so new payments cannot be started and in-flight ones cannot advance. From V4 the ledger still holds the truth, so nothing is lost — the projection is rebuildable, but the write path stops until it is back.
